entries.title: Berlin's punitive measures unlikely to deter Putin: experts
entries.summary: Germany has announced punitive measures after publicly blaming Russia for an attempted airport drone attack. But a former diplomat, political and security analysts warn it will likely do little to deter the Kremlin.
entries.content:
Germany

Berlin's punitive measures unlikely to deter Putin: experts

September 2, 2026

Germany has announced punitive measures after publicly blaming Russia for an attempted airport drone attack. But a former diplomat, political and security analysts warn it will likely do little to deter the Kremlin.

The practical impact of Germany's latest measures against Russia may be limited, according to Russian political scientist Dmitry Oreshkin, who described the response as largely symbolic.

However, Berlin's decision to publicly attribute the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4 to Moscow reflects a growing willingness to respond to Russian President Vladimir Putin and what Berlin sees as hostile actions on its territory.

"It's only a source of joy for Putin. After all, he is restoring this Iron Curtain between Russia and all the other countries. And now he's getting help from the other side as well," Oreshkin told DW. "Putin is someone who cannot be stopped by anything other than escalation and tough restrictions."

Berlin's decision to close the Russian consulate in the western city of Bonn, terminate the contract for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and tighten entry controls for Russian citizens does not go far enough, according to Boris Bondarev, a former diplomat who worked for the Russian permanent mission to the UN Office at Geneva.

Bondarev, who resigned his post in 2022 over Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, said reducing staff and restricting diplomatic activities may complicate Russian operations in Germany, but they will not fundamentally alter Moscow's strategic calculus.

"I'm not sure this will be perceived in Russia as something that will make them think twice," he said. "Unless there are other, more coordinated steps at the EU level, they won't stop provocations. At most, they may force them to coordinate a little differently and look for more professional operatives."

Both experts agreed, however, that Germany's measures could have an effect even if they fail to deter Moscow — by setting off another cycle of reciprocal restrictions.

How will Russia respond?

Speaking on Tuesday, President Putin called Germany's response "another mistake, a serious one," with the Kremlin telling the German Press Agency that Russia would respond "in kind."

German security policy expert Wolfgang Richter said the risk of escalation has increased compared with the early years of the Russia-Ukraine war, but said the next phase of confrontation between Berlin and Moscow is likely to remain in the areas of diplomacy and culture.

"They will, for example, close the Goethe-Institut," said Richter, a colonel with Germany's military until his retirement in 2010. "I would not quite exclude that they could also escalate a little bit and do more — for example, limit the number of diplomats in the German embassy in Moscow."

Former diplomat Bondarev, however, said the Kremlin's reaction could be difficult to predict.

"Moscow officials can surprise you. They could say: 'We have all these people under surveillance anyway, so why expel them? Let them work, and we'll continue monitoring them.' It could go either way. But most likely, there will be some high-profile retaliatory steps," he said.

The dispute over organizations such as the Goethe-Institut and the Russian House in Berlin reflects a deeper divide in how Moscow and Western governments view their role. The Goethe-Institut, founded in 1951 to promote German language and culture abroad, is seen by Moscow through the lens of its broader suspicion of Western institutions, said Oreshkin. And, he added, the Kremlin tends to assume that such organizations serve intelligence purposes because it projects its own security-service worldview onto Western structures.

"The Russian system of thinking among the security services assumes that all Western institutions are organized in exactly the same way. This symmetrical picture of the world is deeply mistaken," he said.

Oreshkin said it's unlikely the Kremlin will escalate much further than the level of diplomacy and culture.

"Launching a missile strike — that's something Putin doesn't have the guts to do. And all these acts of sabotage and subversion — supporting alternative political movements, like Alternative for Germany — they're already doing that anyway," he said. "So I don't think Putin can escalate much beyond that. He can, in fact, escalate the rhetoric, and that's what he's doing."

Real pressure point: Russia's shadow fleet

Announcing the measures on Monday, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters that the EU would continue to work on additional sanctions "in the coming weeks." That included tougher action against Russia's "shadow fleet," though he didn't provide further details.

Russian officials have repeatedly warned that attempts to detain or seize vessels linked to Russia's network of ships ​accused of circumventing fuel sanctions would be regarded as hostile acts.

Oreshkin said if Europe really wants to put pressure on the Kremlin, targeting the financial flows behind the shadow fleet would be more effective. But he pointed to a major obstacle: European governments are constrained by their own legal frameworks, which include maritime law that ensure freedom of navigation.

Security expert Richter, however, sees a broader security risk. Pressure on the shadow fleet could increase the likelihood of incidents at sea, he told DW. "And that would, of course, mean another escalation."

For Richter, the answer lies in making sure both sides understand the risks involved. "The situation has become more tense and it's high time to speak," he said. Without communication between the parties, he warned, any actions could be misinterpreted and might trigger further escalation.

Edited by: Martin Kuebler

entries.title: Unity at last: Is Libya's damaging power struggle at an end?
entries.summary: For over a decade, Libya has been split between two opposing governments. Elections, meant to end the rivalry and unite the country, are now scheduled within two years.
entries.content:
Middle East

Unity at last: Is Libya's damaging power struggle at an end?

September 2, 2026

For over a decade, Libya has been split between two opposing governments. Elections, meant to end the rivalry and unite the country, are now scheduled within two years.

There have been other attempts made in the past but this time, those involved hope it will finally work out: Thanks to mediation by the United Nations, the two opposing governments in the west and east of Libya have agreed that they will hold parliamentary and presidential elections within the next two years.

"The agreement marks an important step in advancing Libya towards national elections and ending the transitional period," the UN's Support Mission in Libya, or UNSMIL, said in a statement.

Among other things, the country's electoral commission will be restructured and, according to the UN, various points about the legal framework for the elections that had previously led to disagreements have now been resolved.

But whether all this will actually result in free and fair elections in Libya remains to be seen.

Divided for over a decade

After former Libyan dictator Moammar Gadhafi was overthrown in 2011, Libya ended up divided in two.

Since 2014, the country has been split between opposing governments located in the east and west of the country. A UN-backed administration known as the Government of National Unity is based in Tripoli in the west, and its rival, known as the House of Representatives, is based in the east, in Tobruk.

Former warlord-turned-politician Khalifa Haftar, is based in the east while Prime Minister Abdul-Hamid Dbeibah is in charge in the west.

Each is supported by a number of local militias and foreign powers, and each has tried to wrest control from the other. Up until now, attempts to hold an election that would unite the country have failed.

For Andreas Dittmann, a geographic conflict expert and professor at the University of Giessen in Hesse, central Germany, the apparent unity is a positive.

"Things could not continue the way they were," he told DW.

After years of civil war and political division, the desire of many Libyans to end the fighting permanently has only grown. Dittmann believes the attitudes of political actors have also changed in this regard.

Previously foreign actors had supported just one Libyan government, but now that has also changed and the prevailing argument seems to be that Libya can only develop further if both sides are incorporated into one administration.

This is why the UN is trying to go beyond simply arranging a date for elections. It also wants to strengthen the electoral commission and work on electoral laws. The new and united government will be responsible for establishing the conditions for a secure and trusted electoral process. 

The UN has also set up what it calls "Structured Dialogues," during which consensus was sought on questions of leadership, security, the economy and reconciliation.

Past agreements didn't work out

Michael Bauer, who heads the Tunisia office of Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, believes the agreement is an important, if limited, step. Its success will depend on how binding any decisions are, he argued.

After all, Bauer said, there have been plenty of political agreements in Libya in the recent past but none were really ever implemented.

Parallel to the UN process, the US is also trying to work on bringing the disparate leadership together. Massad Boulos, the Trump administration's senior adviser on Arab and Middle Eastern affairs, has been trying to bring the Dbeibah and Haftar families together.

In June, Haftar's son Saddam was in Washington where he met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Bauer said the American way of dealing with Libya differentiates from the UN plan. "While the UN mission has basically been very inclusive, in my opinion, the American mission is trying to bring about a kind of deal between the country's elites," he told DW.

He questions how such a deal would fit into free and fair elections in Libya.

"Elections can only be meaningful if the outcome has not already been decided beforehand," Bauer said. The same is true for any pre-election allocation of political positions.

Elites strike a deal?

UK-based think tank Chatham House has already warned that a deal like this, around ministries and resources, will only institutionalize the existing rivalry between Libya's ruling elites. With such an arrangement the rival actors would just divide the state's resources between themselves, and corruption and patronage systems would continue.

The country's division into east and west will be hard to overcome. A new united government would have to deal with preexisting power structures, rather than starting anew.

Dittmann said there is a further problem. Much of the Libyan population lives in the western areas, especially in the Tripoli region. This would see the eastern half of the country lose power if elections are held.

"If there are elections, and if those elections proceed mostly according to democratic principles, then the east can really only lose," he explained.

Additionally, there are also external actors to consider. Russia has extended its positioning in the east while Turkey supports the government in the west.

Alongside all of that is also the question of what the Libyan people want and what they expect from a united government. Bauer doubts elections alone can resolve Libya's problems.

"The people have a particular interest in seeing the country's dysfunction end," he said.

Libya is rich in raw materials and energy reserves, but also plagued by problems like power outages and inadequate public services. If the state was functioning properly, it would likely curtail the power of those currently benefiting most from the country's resources and, as Bauer argued, "why would they voluntarily give up these opportunities?"

That will be the most difficult question for the next two years. The new agreement between Libya's political rivals must do more than simply establish a path toward elections. It must also create a framework in which those rivals accept the results of an election and in which public institutions function properly.

This story was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany: How to woo voters with an immigrant background
entries.summary: The number of voters in Germany with an immigrant background is rising. Yet the established parties barely manage to reach them. Why not?
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: How to woo voters with an immigrant background

September 2, 2026

The number of voters in Germany with an immigrant background is rising. Yet the established parties barely manage to reach them. Why not?

German voters of immigrant background are distancing themselves from the established parties even more than others, according to a study by the Berlin-based German Center for Integration and Migration Research (DeZIM). 

In 2023, 12% of eligible voters in Germany were of immigration background — meaning they or at least one of their parents were born without German citizenship. That amounts to more than seven million people in a population of close to 84 million. But they are drifting away from the traditional centrist parties.

Nevertheless, according to the study, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) continues to have the greatest voter potential among immigrants and their descendants: Two out of three voters with an immigrant background said they considered the SPD a viable option. 

The center-right bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) is close behind in second place. Only one in five respondents categorically rejected these parties.

"Older respondents with an immigrant background lean toward the SPD," said Friederike Römer, co-author of the study, at an online press conference this week. "This bond has been relatively strong in the past, but that seems to be breaking down now among younger generations."

AfD targets migrants

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) has the least potential voters of immigrant background. Nearly two-thirds of those surveyed said voting for the far-right was out of the question. People with roots in Turkey, the Middle East and North Africa, in particular, reject the party, though the AfD does enjoy significant support among Germany's Russian community. 

Nevertheless, the AfD is working to win over the immigrant voter base.

"For a long time, it was the first party to communicate in immigrants' native languages using images that actually worked," said Martin Gerlach, federal executive director of the Turkish Community in Germany (TGD), recalling the AfD campaign in Berlin during the 2021 federal election.

"It read: 'Atatürk would vote for the AfD.' Other parties simply don't bother to think about these target groups. That's crazy, because if you win over big segments of voters with a migration background, you win elections."

Safety a priority for immigrants

The TGD was active in 60 German cities ahead of the last federal election in February 2025, encouraging voters of Turkish background to cast their ballots. But Gerlach has noticed that immigrants are not inherently pro-immigration; on the contrary, there is widespread skepticism toward new immigrants or refugees, an issue that the AfD has seized on. This, he argues, is just one of many reasons why other parties are losing support among those voters.

"The political parties don't address safety at all, and that's a huge issue," he said. "Yet people in our community feel extremely threatened in many parts of Germany — they don't even dare go to the Baltic Sea coast," he added, referring to a series of xenophobic attacks in that region.

Gerlach believes that Islamophobia has a significant effect on voters from the Turkish community, but the centrist parties don't pay enough attention to it.

"Anti-discrimination policy is seen in Germany as something progressive and left-wing, yet for the Turkish-origin community, it is about being protected by the constitution in the truest sense of the word," he said. "I believe this is a narrative that could win over a great many people."

Are the political parties missing a trick on social change?

Political scientist Özgür Özvatan pointed out that by 2030, more than half of Germany's population will have an immigrant background. He has also been critical of the established parties, most recently in his 2025 book "Every Vote Counts — Underestimated by Democrats, Courted by Populists: Migrant Germans as a Political Force."

"They are not reaching out to voters with an immigrant background the way they should — neither to recruit them for their own party, nor as volunteers, nor simply as voters," he said. "Sadly, we're missing the boat with this social change."

Özvatan argues that there is enormous potential to mobilize voters who have moved to Germany from authoritarian countries — people, for example, who have direct experience of trying to defend democracy.

"We can tap into that if we enable them to obtain citizenship with voting rights as quickly as possible," he said.

The AfD, meanwhile, relies on a strategy of addressing the Turkish diaspora while establishing connections to the right-wing authoritarian President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Furthermore, he said, the AfD has become very skilled at pitting people with immigrant backgrounds against one another.

"A great deal of effort is being put into telling older immigrants: 'You are different from the newcomers, this whole debate about migration and deportation won't affect you.' And this tactic works well with those who do not reject the AfD," said Özvatan.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Macron visits Bayeux Tapestry with King Charles, PM Andy Burnham
entries.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron is on a shorter-term visit to the UK than the renowned on-loan 11th century tapestry. He viewed the ancient artwork with the UK monarch and relatively new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

Macron visits Bayeux Tapestry with King Charles, PM Burnham

September 2, 2026

French President Emmanuel Macron is on a shorter-term visit to the UK than the renowned on-loan 11th century tapestry. He viewed the ancient artwork with the UK monarch and relatively new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

French President Emmanuel Macron began a two-day trip to the UK by visiting another famous new arrival from France, the Bayeux Tapestry, with King Charles III and Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Macron and his wife Brigitte, and Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel joined King Charles and Queen Camilla to walk the length of the 70-meter tapestry in the British Museum.

Charles hailed the "unprecedented loan" as a "precious symbol of trust" between the UK and France, while Macron said the two countries were "as close as the threads" in the artwork.

Why is the Bayeux Tapestry in London?

The tapestry, which depicts the momentous events of 1066 culminating in William the Conqueror of Normandy claiming the English throne, is on temporary loan from its usual home in France. It's the first time it's touched British soil since its creation in the 11th century.

The embroidery is on loan for a 10-month exhibiton opening to the public next week, on September 10. The exchange was first announced during Macron's state visit last year.

Though it's thought to have been made in the British Isles, it had been on French soil ever since the 11th century. It's usually on show in Bayeux in Normandy in northern France, hence the name. The effectively priceless artefact was transited across the Channel in secret in July. 

Prime Minister Burnham, who took office six weeks ago, called the tapestry's return "a landmark moment" in the history of the two countries.

He also hailed ties with Macron's French government more generally in the House of Commons on Wednesday, alluding to reduced illegal migration crossings of the English Channel — a bid to counter one of Reform UK's favorite summer talking points.

"The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation — the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low," Burnham said.

It's Macron's first UK visit since Burnham took office and their first in-person meeting as leaders.

What is the Bayeux Tapestry?

The Bayeux Tapestry is a 70-meter long artwork, which is thought to be incomplete, depicting the Norman conquest of England in 1066.

Norman forces led by William the Conqueror were able to defeat and dethrone King Harold Godwinson in a campaign culminating in victory at the Battle of Hastings. The tapestry famously depicts Harold being shot in the eye with an arrow, as he is said to have died — admittedly in what modern historians believe is likely a myth or artistic exaggeration.

This conquest was a crucial contributing moment in the establishment of what would become England and later the British Empire and the UK. It was the last of several successful foreign invasions of England in a millenium, and turned out to be the last one for a millenium.

The conquest also added the final core ingredient, French, to the linguistic melting pot that produced the modern English language.

The embroidered cloth, which has brief Latin titles captioning its 58 scenes, is widely accepted to have been made in England as a tribute to William after his victory. It was then transported to his family home in Normandy.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Russia's hybrid attacks on Germany: When is it 'war?'
entries.summary: The German government is holding Russia responsible for an unsuccessful attack in Leipzig. Yet many feel that its response has been too mild.
entries.content:
Germany

Russia's hybrid attacks on Germany: When is it 'war?'

September 2, 2026

The German government is holding Russia responsible for an unsuccessful attack in Leipzig. Yet many feel that its response has been too mild.

Fortunately, nothing bad happened this time around. Had the attack succeeded, however, who knows what the consequences might have been: On the evening of August 4, a drone outfitted with explosives and a detonation device was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport. The airport serves as a hub for military aid to Ukraine.

The German government hesitated for a long time before publicly holding Russia responsible. But now it has announced its findings.

On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters that the methods used in the attempted attack were consistent with those seen in other Russian hybrid operations, citing the drone's construction, various components, explosives and detonation technology.

He noted that the attack had been planned with a "high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort."

In late August, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said of the incident: "The federal government will make the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this."

At the time, he did not mention Russia by name. And even now, Merz himself has not commented on the matter.

However, the price Russia will have to pay is relatively small. The Russian House cultural institute in Berlin is being shut down amid suspicions that it is serving as a cover for espionage. The Russian Consulate General in Bonn is also being closed. What's more, entry requirements for Russian citizens are set to be tightened, and Germany also plans to take tougher action against the Russian "shadow fleet" — the network of ships ​accused of circumventing fuel sanctions. Exactly how and when remains unclear, however.

Mixed reactions to Germany's measures

For the environmentalist Green Party in the Bundestag, however, the government's response was lacking.

"The federal government's analysis came a bit late, and the steps it's taking aren't enough for me," said Sara Nanni, the Greens' security policy spokesperson, in a DW interview. "I don't think anyone in Moscow is afraid or giving it a second thought right now."

As an example, she said Germany should be taking tougher action against the Russian shadow fleet. This would be necessary to "stop the flow of money to the Russian war machine," she said.

Roderich Kiesewetter, security expert with Chancellor Merz' center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), is also dissatisfied. In the Handelsblatt newspaper, he called for the delivery of Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine — and for the activation of Article 4 of the NATO Treaty, which requires allies to engage into consultations in the event of an external threat.

He urged the German government to abandon "the politically convenient path of appeasement."

However, wouldn't responding more assertively, as Kiesewetter has demanded, risk provoking a military confrontation with Russia, especially given that Russia has flatly denied responsibility for the Leipzig incident?

On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin called the German sanctions against his country a "serious mistake" and accused Germany of fabricating evidence. The Foreign Ministry in Moscow announced that it would take countermeasures.

Foreign Minister Wadephul sees Germany as a target

Once again, the question of whether Germany is already at war with Russia is being raised — and this time with even greater urgency. But the federal government has unequivocally denied it.

"We are not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday, after he blamed Russia for the failed attack.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told German public broadcaster ARD that Germany is not at war but is a Russian "war target."

A year ago, in September 2025, Chancellor Merz said — though without naming Russia: "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either."

This came against the backdrop of increasing attacks on data networks, critical infrastructure and hybrid threats.

Security expert Sönke Marahrens from the University of Kiel offered a more nuanced answer: "No, Germany is not at war at the moment. We are facing hybrid activities by other countries, but we are not at war."

In Western countries, he noted, declarations of war are regulated by law. And in Germany, according to the constitution, the Bundestag must declare that the country is at war, and that applies only after a physical attack.

"Nothing currently meets that definition," he said.

However, the Green Party's Nanni fears Russia will continue to escalate the situation.

"We are not yet at war with Russia, but Russia appears to be preparing for a war not only against Ukraine but against all of Europe," she said, calling the incident in Leipzig an "attempted terrorist act."

Not at war with Russia

From a legal standpoint, too, Germany is not at war with Russia. No declaration of war has been made, no recognized armed conflict exists, and no collective defense obligation has been invoked under NATO's Article 5. Furthermore, consultations among NATO members, which must take place before a collective defense obligation can be invoked, have not been scheduled under Article 4.

But things look different when it comes to hybrid warfare, which is not as precisely defined. Numerous security experts have argued that Russia is already waging just such a hybrid war against Western nations. This refers to attacks on infrastructure, cyberattacks, disinformation and traditional espionage.

However, the line between hybrid war and an open act of war are blurry. Marahrens believes Russia is using hybrid actions — such as the one in Leipzig — to advance its strategic interests in Germany, the second-most important supporter of Ukraine after the US. Had the attack at the airport been successful, it would have relieved pressure on the Russian front, Marahrens said.

He went on to say that "if Russia succeeds in convincing the German public not to support these political decisions [to support Ukraine], that would also directly reduce the pressure on the front lines."

AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine

The state election on Sunday in Saxony-Anhalt is one current example of Russian strategic interests. Many observers believe that this election is the most important in Germany in decades.

The key question is whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which is classified as far right by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency — will secure an absolute majority and, for the first time, govern a German state.

The AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine and would like to normalize relations with Russia. This resonates with many in eastern Germany, where the war in Ukraine is seen by many as none of Germany's business, and where there is a feeling that too much money has already been sent to Ukraine.

This is why the federal government — composed of the conservative CDU/CSU bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — is being careful about stepping up its rhetoric, as doing so could potentially help the AfD secure an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt. On the other hand, it can hardly afford to place the blame for the events in Leipzig on Russia while also responding in only a relatively mild manner.

This dilemma may also be the reason why Chancellor Merz has so far refrained from speaking out to blame Russia.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Austria women ice hockey team fight for future generations
entries.summary: Austria are getting ready for their first Women's Ice Hockey World Championship. But preparations have been overshadowed by a dispute about conditions, pay and getting men's cast-off kit. A solution now looks in sight.
entries.content:
September 2, 2026

Austria are getting ready for their first Women's Ice Hockey World Championship. But preparations have been overshadowed by a dispute about conditions, pay and getting men's cast-off kit. A solution now looks in sight.

When the Austrian women's national ice hockey team took to the ice in the Women's European Cup of Nations in Slovakia in August, they did so without 11 of their top players.

Captain Anna Meixner and the rest of her team were frustrated that the Austrian Ice Hockey Association (ÖEHV) still hadn't responded to a list of grievances outlined in a letter to the organization last March. Meixner stresses that the players only went public with their complaints as something of a last resort.

Among the nine complaints on their list of demands were the standard of accommodation, having to change in unheated dressing rooms in the winter and not being paid per diems during training camps and international tournaments. They also said they had to make do with hand-me-down equipment from the men's team.

"We really tried to respect the federation (ÖEHV) and we really tried to solve it from within, without outside noise," Meixner told DW in a Zoom interview on Wednesday.

"So we had been fighting for four or five months without going out to the newspapers. But when we realized that nothing had changed, we had to take the next step."

"The final straw, if you want to call it that, was a camp last February. It was the no-heater-in-the-locker-room situation," said the 32-year-old forward, who, after two seasons in North America's PWHL (Professional Women's Hockey League)  with the Ottawa Charge and Vancouver Goldeneyes, is returning to her previous team, Swedish outfit Brynas, for 2026-27.

"Here were people that had been sitting on a train for 14 hours, who didn't get food when they arrived. We had to go on the ice straight away. So, I think that was when it really became clear to us that enough is enough."

Fighting for future generations of women in hockey

Meixner also stressed that their aim was primarily to improve things for the women's national team in the longer term.

"We have this older generation right now and we're not going to play for the national team forever. We really felt it's time to give the next generation everything that we didn't have over the last 10 to 15 years. We brought it up with the team and everybody was on board right away."

To rachet up the pressure on the ÖEHV, the players also threatened to boycott the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship in Denmark in November ― a significant moment, as this is the first time Austria have qualified for the top IIHF (International Ice Hockey Federation) tournament.

"Going to the newspapers," as Meixner put it, seems to have worked.

In a press release following last month's tournament in Slovakia, in which Austria came second out of the four teams, the ÖEHV said it had taken the opportunity to hold "constructive conversations" with the players.

Now, Meixner appears cautiously optimistic.

Demands starting to be met

"We have gotten some answers from the federation and we are just in the process of going over everything. But now, we're happy about the direction things seem to be moving in," said Meixner, who added that the players and federation were finally speaking on an equal footing.

"It feels like they [the ÖEHV] actually want to change something. If it stays that way, I'm sure we can figure something out and make it work. Because obviously the last thing we want to do is to miss the World Championship."

Indeed, in a letter to the team sent on August 31, the ÖEHV responded to each of their nine demands outlining specific steps that had either already been implemented or were in the works.

These include a pledge to implement "clear regulations regarding per diems/remuneration and the timely payment of bonuses and travel expenses," to provide "adequate accommodation and reliable, needs-based catering" for training camps, "adequate cabin and gym facilities" as well as "sufficient time for travel and recovery."

Battling for 'bare minimums'

It also notes that it would seek a "teamwear solution" as part of a new contract with the association's equipment provider.

While this all seems promising, Meixner still finds it frustrating that in 2026, she and her teammates have had to battle so hard for what she termed "bare minimums."

At the same time though, she said that if the players and the ÖEHV do actually manage to put aside their dispute, it will be bigger than everything she has achieved on the ice ― including winning the tournament in China last year that put Austria through to a first Women's Ice Hockey Championship.

"I'm unbelievably proud of us for staying hard at it for many months. There are so many girls from other nations reaching out saying, 'you know what? It's great that you're doing that and we should do the same,'" she said.

"We've heard the men's team stepping up, cheering for us. I think this is bigger than hockey. Hopefully this will be a big step for Austrian women's sports and Austrian women in general."

Unless an unforeseen hitch arises over the next few weeks, Austria will open their first-ever World Championship campaign against Czechia in Esbjerg, Denmark on November 6.

Mathias Brück contributed to this report.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

entries.title: US sanctions halt TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran, disrupting study plans
entries.summary: Students in Iran can no longer take TOEFL and GRE exams after a US sanctions exemption was suspended. Applicants say the move threatens university deadlines and adds costly travel obligations.
entries.content:
September 2, 2026

Students in Iran can no longer take TOEFL and GRE exams after a US sanctions exemption was suspended. Applicants say the move threatens university deadlines and adds costly travel obligations.

Iranian students hoping to study abroad are facing a new obstacle after TOEFL and GRE testing was suspended inside the country following changes to US sanctions regulations.

"My entire plan was built around taking this exam," a TOEFL candidate in Tehran told DW.

She said she had spent months preparing applications for a PhD program, contacting professors and gathering documents despite internet disruptions and other challenges.

ETS, the US-based organization that administers both exams, announced it suspended testing in Iran after the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) froze General License G, which had allowed certain educational services to continue in Iran.

"Following OFAC's suspension of General License G, ETS has paused administration of the TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran effective immediately," the organization said in an official notice.

ETS added that Iranian nationals can still take the exams outside Iran and that it is exploring options to restore testing.

TOEFL is a US-based English-language proficiency test accepted by universities worldwide. The GRE is a standardized test required by some graduate programs, particularly in the United States and Canada.

Since the Iran war began in late February, the US has increasingly expanded sanctions targeting Iranian trade and exports, contributing to broader disruptions throughout the Iranian economy.

No timeline for testing to resume

An Iranian institution that administered TOEFL exams told DW that new registrations had stopped following the latest sanctions changes.

The institution added that the suspension could be temporary, but no date had been given for exams to resume.

That uncertainty is particularly serious for students approaching university and scholarship deadlines who have spent months preparing and paying application-related costs.

The suspension follows earlier problems with IELTS (British equivalent of TOEFL) testing in Iran. An IELTS center in Tehran told DW that sanctions-related difficulties transferring money had become one of the main obstacles to continuing exams.

Some Iranian applicants had already been traveling to countries such as Turkey and Armenia to take IELTS. TOEFL and GRE candidates may now have to do the same.

Rising costs for applicants

Alireza, who is preparing to apply to a university in Italy, said the suspension of TOEFL had disrupted a backup plan he had arranged after IELTS testing became unavailable.

"European universities usually accept IELTS. But because IELTS has been suspended in Iran, after extensive correspondence with the university, they agreed to let [Iranian students] meet the required score through an equivalent TOEFL result," he told DW.

"But now TOEFL has also been suspended in Iran. Traveling to a neighboring country just to take the exam is very expensive, especially given Iran's current economic situation," added Alireza.

Another candidate told DW that taking the exam in Turkey or Armenia would mean paying for travel and at least one night's accommodation on top of the test fee.

For students hoping to secure scholarships or full funding, those additional expenses can be significant.

Students launch petition

Iranian TOEFL and GRE candidates have launched an online petition urging ETS to restore access to the exams.

The petition says thousands of students are losing access to tests required for university admissions, scholarships, graduate programs and other academic opportunities. Many, it says, have spent months preparing, paid exam-related costs and built their application schedules around specific test dates.

"Students should not lose years of preparation or their chance to pursue higher education because access to required examinations has suddenly been removed," the petition states.

Narges, an Iranian applicant affected by the suspension, said she had seen the petition circulating in Telegram groups used by language learners and students applying to foreign universities.

"I doubt it will have any impact," she said. "Still, I'm going to sign the petition."

The organizers are calling on OFAC to provide a specific exemption for standardized academic testing, and on ETS to restore TOEFL and GRE services in Iran as soon as legally possible.

They argue that sanctions aimed at the Iranian government should not restrict educational opportunities for ordinary citizens who have no role in state policy.

When sanctions impact education

Until recently, the General License G had provided a legal channel for certain academic exchanges and educational services despite broader US sanctions on Iran.

For many students, the suspension is the latest in a series of barriers to studying abroad.

Bahar, who is applying for PhD programs, said many Iranian students had already shifted their focus from the United Statesbecause obtaining visas had become increasingly difficult.

"American universities were our first choice because they generally offer funding for PhD programs more readily than European universities," she told DW.

Now, she said, applicants are increasingly turning to Europe and Australia, but the testing suspension has created a new hurdle.

"There is effectively no difference between IELTS and TOEFL for us now, because in either case, we have to leave Iran to take an English language test," Bahar said.

For students approaching admissions deadlines, postponement may not simply mean waiting a few months. It can mean missing an entire admissions cycle, losing scholarship opportunities or delaying academic plans by a year or more.

While ETS says it is examining possible ways to restore testing in Iran, there is currently no indication of when that might happen. For many applicants, the immediate choice is limited: wait without knowing when testing will return, or spend considerably more to take the same exam abroad.

Edited by: Ole Tangen Jr

entries.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy warns airlines to avoid Russian airspace
entries.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned a surge in Ukrainian drones in Russia's skies meant Russian airspace would be "effectively" closed. Meanwhile, Russian drones have hit Kyiv for a seventh straight day. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Zelenskyy warns airlines to avoid Russian airspace

Published September 2, 2026last updated September 2, 2026

Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned a surge in Ukrainian drones in Russia's skies meant Russian airspace would be "effectively" closed. Meanwhile, Russian drones have hit Kyiv for a seventh straight day. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Read below for the latest developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on Wednesday, September 2.

  • Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns drone surge is making Russian airspace unsafe for civil aviation
  • Zelenskyy also says Germany and Ukraine are finalizing a drone deal
  • Two civilians reported killed in Russian attacks on central Ukrainian city of Dnipro

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Germany says EU countries handing out too many visas to Russians

Germany says EU countries handing out too many visas to Russians

Berlin is pushing for other EU members to cut down on tourist visas to Russian citizens, essentially calling for stricter rules across the entire EU.

More than 600,000 short-stay visas were issued by EU countries in Russia last year. Italy, France and Spain issued the most, while Germany approved a mere 20,000.

Berlin says it wants to make sure that people who could pose a security risk are not allowed to enter the EU.

The call comes as tensions between Germany and Russia peak over Berlin’s accusation that Moscow was the mastermind behind an attempted drone attack a German airport in August.

Skip next section Russian ship seized in Norway

Russian ship seized in Norway

Norway has seized a Russian ship due to a request by Ukrainian state company Naftogaz, the company said.

According to Naftogaz — which has been looking for compensation from Russia since 2016 due to its expropriation of Naftogaz property — the seizure was meant to ensure that Russia meets its outstanding obligations.

It was ordered by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court.

The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was Russia-owned.

"Russia cannot evade responsibility by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award, " Naftogaz's acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko said.

Skip next section Belgium's position on frozen Russian assets unchanged

Belgium's position on frozen Russian assets unchanged

Belgium's opposition to using frozen Russian assets has remained in place, the country's foreign minister said.

This comes after several European Union countries called the bloc to move forward with the move last week.

According to Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot, the idea "generated little enthusiasm" among the bloc's foreign ministers, adding the Brussels government's objection to the move stems from reasons that "have not magically disappeared."

About 210 billion euros (243.4 billion dollars) of Russian assets were immobilized following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Belgium last year rejected the European Commission's proposal to use the assets for a loan to Ukraine due to fears it would not be singled out by potential lawsuits by Russia.

Skip next section READ MORE: Should Germany intensify its response after the failed Leipzig attack?

READ MORE: Should Germany intensify its response after the failed Leipzig attack?

The German government is holding Russia responsible for an unsuccessful attack in Leipzig. Yet many feel that its response has been too mild.

Read the full story: Russia's hybrid attacks on Germany: When is it 'war?'

Skip next section Pressure on Russia to grow, EU foreign policy chief says

Pressure on Russia to grow, EU foreign policy chief says

The European Union's foreign policy head Kaja Kallas said the bloc is interested in tightening the enforcement of sanctions against Russia.

The move should also come with increasing pressure on Moscow, as well as increasing support for Ukraine.

"Attempts to intimidate Europe will fail," Kallas said.

 

Skip next section Childrens' hospice founder arrested after war criticism

Childrens' hospice founder arrested after war criticism

The founder of a Russianchildren's hospice has been detained and charged with deliberately spreading false information about the war in Ukraine.

Lida Moniava, who is known for her engagement for sick children, took to Telegram to call the war a crime and said it must end.

According to Russian investigators, Moniava posted false information "presented as credible reports" about the Russian army's actions against civilian population in Ukraine.

The childrens' hospice Moniava founded in Moscow said it will continue to operate as usual, without adding further information.

Skip next section EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig attack

EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig attack

The European Union's foreign policy head Kaja Kallas summoned the Russian envoy in Brussels following Germany's announcement that Russia was behind the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport last month.

Skip next section WATCH: Why are books becoming a casualty of war in Ukraine?

WATCH: Why are books becoming a casualty of war in Ukraine?

Skip next section Ukraine says Russian airspace 'not safe' amid drone surge

Ukraine says Russian airspace 'not safe' amid drone surge

Kyiv says it has formally notified the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) that Russian airspace is "not safe" as a result of increasing Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian territory.

Ukraine has also asked the UN agency to prohibit member countries from using Russian airspace, according to a government letter to the ICAO cited by Reuters.

It came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines to stay away.

"We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia's skies are over," Zelenskyy said.

"Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation," he added. "The sky over Russia is currently for drones ... as long as the war continues."

Last week, Zelenskyy threatened to deploy up to 1,000 long-range drones per day.

The ICAO has not commented on the request from Ukraine.

Russia's aviation watchdog regularly closes airports in response to the Ukrainian drones. Ukraine's airspace has been closed since the war started in 2022.

While European ​and US carriers do not fly over Russia due to the conflict, the airspace is used by other airlines from China, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf countries.

Russia has stepped up its strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities in recent weeks. Ukraine has responded with long-range drone strikes on Russian energy and military infrastructure.

Skip next section Kyiv under attack for 7th straight day, 2 civilians killed in Dnipro

Kyiv under attack for 7th straight day, 2 civilians killed in Dnipro

Russian drones hit central Kyiv for a seventh day in a row on Wednesday, injuring seven people and damaging residential and university buildings, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

The attack on a downtown university forced some 160 people to take shelter, he added.

Also on Wednesday, Russia struck electricity facilities in the southern Odesa region, knocking out power to more than 350,000 homes, authorities said.

Two people were also killed and eight wounded in Russian strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro, officials said.

According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia fired 174 attack drones, as well as two ballistic missiles and two plane-launched missiles at Ukraine overnight.

Meanwhile, Russia said its air defenses destroyed 130 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Ukrainian drone attacks on Wednesday killed two people in Russia's Belgorod border region and wounded 16 more, officials said.

Skip next section Ukraine and Germany close to inking drone deal, Zelenskyy says

Ukraine and Germany close to inking drone deal, Zelenskyy says

Ukraine is close to finalizing a drone deal with Germany, President Volodymyr ‌Zelenskyy ⁠said ⁠on Wednesday after a call with ​German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

"This will, ​among other ‌things, certainly enhance the defense capabilities of both Germany and ​Ukraine," the Ukrainian president wrote on Telegram.

The agreement, initially proposed by Ukraine several months ago, is expected to involve the joint development of several types of drones, missiles and related software.

Zelenskyy thanked Germany and said he would meet with the chancellor to sign the deal in person.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned airlines to avoid Russian airspace amid a surge in Ukrainian drone activity.

Kyiv formally notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace was "not safe."

Moscow, in response, said it was improving flight safety and would not allow Ukraine to seriously disrupt aviation.

More than four years after Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the two countries continue to trade daily strikes.

Russian attacks on Wednesday killed two civilians and wounded six in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials said, while the capital Kyiv was targeted for a seventh day in a row.

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said he held a call with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and that their two countries were close to finalizing a drone deal.

We'll be following these developments, along with other key events in Russia's war against Ukraine, throughout the day in this blog.

entries.title: Guinea-Bissau referendum tests democratic future
entries.summary: Following voter approval of a constitutional change that expands presidential powers, Guinea-Bissau faces renewed debate over legitimacy, civilian rule and democratic safeguards.
entries.content:
Guinea-Bissau

Guinea-Bissau referendum tests democratic future

September 2, 2026

Following voter approval of a constitutional change that expands presidential powers, Guinea-Bissau faces renewed debate over legitimacy, civilian rule and democratic safeguards.

Guinea-Bissau is facing a new political test after voters approved a referendum on a proposed charter that will give the president the power to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and government ministers, while reducing the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65..

Sunday's referendum came less than 10 months after a coup in which the military seized power and three months ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled to take place on December 6.

The transitional authorities say the constitutional reform is intended to bring stability to the impoverished West African country and prepare it for a return to civilian rule.

Victory claimed, legitimacy disputed

On Monday, the National Transitional Council claimed victory for the "Yes" camp. "The majority of those who went to vote voted yes. In conclusion, the victory of yes is guaranteed," council spokesman Alberto Pinto Pereira said.

On Tuesday, the National Electoral Commission (NEC) confirmed victory for the "Yes" side, saying it had received 70% of the vote, compared with 30% for the "No" camp, and that voter turnout exceeded 50%.

NEC chairperson Carmen Izaura Lobo described the Guinea-Bissau referendum as a success, due to the "organizational capacity, professionalism and dedication" of teams on the ground, Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported.

Lobo praised the "transparency" and "credibility" of the process.

The opposition, however, says the referendum has no legal basis because it was organized by institutions created after the military coup. It had called on voters to boycott the vote.

Domingos Simoes Pereira, leader of the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), who was detained after the military coup and later released into house arrest, rejected the referendum as legally invalid.

Speaking to DW from Portugal, he said the institutions established by the military have no democratic mandate to rewrite Guinea-Bissau's constitution.

The PAIGC and other opposition groups maintain that the vote is a continuation of the November coup.

Fernando Dias Costa, the main challenger to then-President Umaro Sissoco Embalo in the November 2025 presidential election that was annulled by the military, disputed the official turnout figures.

"Very few citizens took part in this referendum," he said, noting that the people have sent an important message that must not be ignored.

"They are not prepared to simply accept political changes that are clearly unconstitutional and have not been publicly debated."

More power for the president

The proposed constitution would move Guinea-Bissau toward a much stronger presidential system. The president would appoint and dismiss the prime minister and government ministers and would have the power to dissolve parliament.

Supporters argue that the existing political system has repeatedly led to conflicts between the president, government and parliament. They say stronger presidential authority would create greater stability.

Bubacar Ture, head of the Guinea-Bissau Human Rights League, told DW that the draft constitution would lead to "an excessive concentration of power in the person of the president."

He argues that the proposed system could make parliamentary elections less meaningful because the president would have much greater control over the government regardless of the parliamentary balance.

Ture also criticizes the way the constitution was drafted. "No one was consulted," he said. "Neither the parties nor civil-society organizations, nor traditional or religious authorities. Everything was produced in secret."

He is particularly concerned that provisions concerning constitutional oversight have been removed. In his view, this would weaken the rule of law.

Supporters and critics view the referendum through the lens of the political crisis that began in November 2025, when both former President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias claimed victory in a disputed presidential election.

Before the results could be officially announced, the military seized power.

Embalo was briefly detained and subsequently left the country. His current whereabouts are unclear, and speculation continues over whether he retains influence over the military leadership or could seek a political comeback.

The referendum in Guinea-Bissau also reflects a broader trend across parts of Africa, where constitutional reforms have sparked debate over the concentration of presidential power.

In recent years, countries including Togo, Chad, Uganda, Zimbabwe and Guinea have seen leaders pursue constitutional changes that critics say strengthen executive authority.

What comes next in Guinea-Bissau?

Despite the "Yes" vote, opposition and civil society groups continue to challenge the legitimacy of the process. The referendum also takes place against a backdrop of longstanding political instability.

Guinea-Bissau has experienced repeated coups and attempted coups since independence, contributing to recurring periods of political instability.

The December elections are intended to mark the return to civilian rule. But opposition criticism of Sunday's referendum has raised further questions about how difficult that transition may be.

A key point of contention is whether the new constitutional order will strengthen democratic institutions or concentrate more power in the presidency.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: India rejects Hague ruling on Indus waters: What's next?
entries.summary: By rejecting an international arbitration panel's ruling, New Delhi has cast fresh doubt on the future of the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty.
entries.content:
India

India rejects Hague ruling on Indus waters: What's next?

September 2, 2026

By rejecting an international arbitration panel's ruling, New Delhi has cast fresh doubt on the future of the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty.

The Indus Waters Treaty is facing a fresh dispute after India rejected a Hague-based Court of Arbitration ruling that the 1960 agreement remains in force.

Pakistan has welcomed the decision and said India remains bound by the treaty.

India's Ministry of External Affairs described the tribunal as a "so-called Court of Arbitration" that was "illegally constituted."

It said the body had been established by the World Bank in breach of the treaty and that India "categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body."

"The Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India's sovereign decisions," the ministry said.

What to know about the treaty

The Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank, governs the use of water from six rivers flowing through India and Pakistan.

The agreement largely gives India rights over three eastern rivers while Pakistan has rights over the western Indus, Jhelum and Chenab. India is allowed to use the western rivers for specified purposes including certain hydroelectric projects.

The treaty had endured wars and prolonged periods of intense hostility between the two nuclear-armed neighbors.

But India placed the treaty in abeyance in April 2025 as part of a package of diplomatic and economic measures announced after a deadly attack in India-administered Kashmir killed 26 people, mostly tourists.

New Delhi accused Islamabad of backing the attack. Pakistan has denied the charges.

High stakes for Pakistan

Millions of people in Pakistan depend on the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers for drinking water, farming and daily life.

The rivers are particularly important to Punjab and Sindh provinces, whose agriculture is central to the country's food supply and rural economy.

After India's move to suspend the treaty, Pakistan approached the court in The Hague over the status of the accord.

Pakistani officials have repeatedly warned that any attempt to deny the country its share of the waters of rivers flowing across the border would be treated as an act of war.

Ajay Bisaria, a former Indian high commissioner to Pakistan, said India had challenged the treaty on both political and legal grounds.

"Politically, abeyance hands India a new point of leverage, one more lever to press Pakistan into changing its behavior on cross-border terrorism," Bisaria told DW.

He also pointed to India's earlier requests to renegotiate the treaty, citing climate change, new dam-building technology and the deterioration of relations between the two countries.

India chose to put the treaty in abeyance rather than formally abrogate it. Bisaria said the ruling in The Hague would not change that course.

"The tribunal will not alter this trajectory," he said. "India's course on the Indus Waters Treaty is set. The treaty will not be revived in its present form."

Legal battle over water

Pakistan has taken the opposite view.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said the ruling "decisively rejects" India's attempt to place the treaty in abeyance and reaffirmed that it remains "fully in force and binding on both parties."

"The Award vindicates Pakistan's consistent position that a binding international treaty cannot be unilaterally suspended or set aside," Dar said in a post on X.

He added that India must comply with its obligations under the treaty and with binding decisions arising from its dispute settlement mechanisms.

Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani political scientist and defense analyst, said the ruling may be difficult to implement if India refuses to accept it.

"The arbitration court's ruling may not be implementable because the court doesn't have the force to do so," Siddiqa told DW.

But she said the decision gave Pakistan an advantage as a lower riparian state.

"It does give Pakistan a moral edge," said Siddiqa, a senior fellow in the Department of War Studies at King's College London.

She also questioned what India's rejection of the ruling could mean for its international position, particularly given that India has accepted international legal decisions in other disputes.

"This is not just an issue of pure military power but an international standing where India will not be able to justify its position to the world any longer," she said.

Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, a South Asia analyst and founder of the Mantraya think tank, said the ruling did not materially change India's position.

"The Permanent Court of Arbitration is an administrative body, not a conventional sovereign court with enforcement capabilities," D'Souza told DW.

"In this particular case, India chose not to participate in the proceedings. This allows it not to recognize the tribunal's rulings. Therefore, it has no enforceable constraint on India and nothing changes materially for New Delhi," she said.

A dispute over the rules

India and Pakistan have disagreed for years over the interpretation of the treaty, particularly over Indian hydropower projects on rivers allocated primarily to Pakistan.

Uttam Kumar Sinha, a senior fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies in New Delhi and author of "Trial by Water," said India is now no longer merely contesting the interpretation of the treaty, but rather "contesting the authority of the treaty's dispute-settlement mechanism itself."

New Delhi maintains that the tribunal was improperly constituted and that its decisions have no legal effect on India.

Sinha described the emerging contest as "lawfare," with Pakistan likely to use the ruling in international forums and frame the dispute around treaty obligations and international law.

The limits of India's leverage

The practical implications will also depend on what India does with its infrastructure on the western rivers.

D'Souza said the treaty's abeyance gave India more political and psychological leverage than an immediate ability to alter the flow of the rivers.

"To effectively stop or significantly alter the flows of the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers, substantial infrastructure like dams, canals and large storage systems would be required, and such structures do not currently exist," said D'Souza.

"Furthermore, geographical and technical constraints limit India's capacity to block these rivers."

Sinha echoed this view.

"India cannot simply 'turn off' the western rivers," he said.

Large storage and diversion projects would take years or decades, require substantial investment and involve difficult construction in the mountainous Himalayan region, as well as environmental and domestic approvals.

"There is a significant gap between India's potential strategic freedom on the western rivers and its actual physical capacity to change water flows," Sinha said.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru
